title: Service and salesmanship at the Master level
lead: The Master practical in the dining room: aperitifs and the start of the meal, glassware for every drink and room, spirits with proper portions, and handling questions and complaints with diplomacy.

lines.label: The Court's ask
lines.text: Handle questions and complaints with skill, elegance and diplomacy, and recommend wines for a wide range of foods, vintages included.

lines.label: Three steps
lines.text: The 2025 standards reduce problem resolution to three moves: acknowledge, apologize, and act quickly and kindly.

know: If a guest rejects a wine, apologize, remove it and check it away from the table: flawed means another bottle of the same, sound means the list.
A wrong bottle or price on the check goes to upper management.
Suggesting a pricier bottle needs a clear reason it's worth more.
If you don't know an answer, offer to find out; never make one up.
The Court's Code of Ethics treats knowingly serving counterfeit wine, or swapping what's in a pre-opened bottle, as a breach of integrity.

facts.fact: The minimum passing score for each of the three sections of the Master Sommelier Diploma Examination is 75%.
MS practical: discuss, recommend and serve aperitifs, with thorough knowledge of their ingredients and production methods and the ability to serve them correctly.
MS practical: select, prepare and position glassware for all beverages in the lounge, restaurant or private function room.
MS practical: discuss menu content and wine list, recommending wines for a wide range of foods, with sound knowledge of products, vintages and characteristics.
MS practical: present, offer, prepare (decanting when necessary) and serve wines efficiently and proficiently.
MS practical: present, offer, prepare and serve brandies, liqueurs and other spirits, including knowledge of the proper serving portions for each.
MS practical: handle questions and complaints with skill, elegance and diplomacy.

The example MS Practical & Tasting feedback report lists Practical results for a Sparkling table, a Decanting table and Business of the Sommelier, and an example comment says mixology was nicely done.

Aperitif wine (27 CFR 4.21(g)): wine of not less than 15% alcohol by volume, compounded from grape wine containing added brandy or alcohol, flavored with herbs and other natural aromatic flavoring materials; designated 'aperitif wine' unless designated 'vermouth'. Vermouth is a type of aperitif wine.

Aperitifs and digestifs are traditionally served from a tray or gueridon; service method, temperature and glassware should match the beverage and guest preference; confirm how the guest would like the drink served before pouring; if uncertain, offer options with brief descriptions.

Side station pouring: pour with a jigger when available, add ice if requested, bring on a tray from the guest's right, confirm the order. Tableside: glassware and accompaniments (water back, side rocks) to the guest's right, present the bottle with the label facing the guest, pour on the tray or at the table.

Gueridon service is used in fine dining; beverages are prepared and served tableside in full view of the guests. Mise en place: clean linen-lined gueridon, one folded serviette, jigger, glassware, ice bucket, tongs, distilled or mineral water, service tray.
Taking the order: identify the host, the guest leading or overseeing the table, who may or may not place the order; stand to the right of the guest ordering; repeat the order back.

Cocktail service: do not add carbonated ingredients before shaking; for drinks on the rocks, use fresh ice, never 'dirty rocks' used in the shaker; built cocktails go in the serving glass in recipe order.

Glassware placement: bring glasses on a tray, place with the right hand on the guest's right, same position for every guest (usually by the knife), start with the host or the guest to the host's left, go clockwise regardless of gender; multiple glasses in a line, diagonal, diamond or cluster; a second bottle of the same wine gets a clean tasting glass for the host, placed to the right of the original glass.
Sparkling service: flutes or wine glasses according to the guest's preference; two serviettes and two underliners (bottle and cork).
Decanting for sediment: three serviettes; three underliners at the table for cork, bottle and decanter.

Beer glassware: Pilsner flute for pilsner; weizen glass for hefeweizen, dunkelweizen and wheat beers; goblet or snifter for Belgian strong and Trappist ales; tulip for IPA, barleywine, imperial stout, porter; American pint for most other styles; AP wine glasses suit many beer styles.
Modern sake service often uses all-purpose or white wine glasses; traditional mori koboshi service pours into an ochoko set in a masu.

Aperitif and digestif glassware: small tulip or copita for fortified wines, grappa, eau de vie and neat liqueurs; rocks glass for liqueurs or spirits over ice; snifter for neat oak-aged spirits such as brandy, aged rum and Calvados.

Brandy (27 CFR 5.145): distilled from the fermented juice, mash or wine of fruit, or its residue, at less than 95% ABV, bottled at not less than 40% ABV (80 proof). Grape brandy stored at least 2 years in oak is 'grape brandy' or 'brandy'; under 2 years, 'immature grape brandy' or 'immature brandy'. 'Brandy' without qualification is only for grape brandy.

Cognac, Armagnac, Brandy de Jerez, Calvados and Pisco are defined by the laws of their country of manufacture; grape pomace brandy (from skins and pulp after the juice is withdrawn) may be called grappa.

Cordials and liqueurs (27 CFR 5.150): flavored distilled spirits made with fruits, flowers, plants or other natural flavorings, with sugar of not less than 2.5% by weight; may be labeled 'dry' if sugar is under 10% by weight.

A US standard drink holds about 0.6 fl oz (14 g) of pure alcohol: 1.5 oz of distilled spirits at about 40%; 2-3 oz of cordial, liqueur or aperitif at about 24%; 3-4 oz of fortified wine at about 17%; 5 oz of table wine at about 12%.
Sweet wines: a by-the-glass serving is usually 2 oz.
Fortified wines: by-the-glass pours are typically 2 oz.
Cognac age categories: at least 2 years (VS / Very Special), at least 4 years (VSOP), at least 10 years (XO); Cognac ages only in oak.

Problem resolution, 2025 standards: acknowledge the issue and listen actively; apologize sincerely, focusing on how it made the guest feel; act quickly and kindly. Suggesting a more expensive option must come with a clear explanation of added value.

Demeanor: don't make things up; offer to get the answer. Discreetly determine budget; offer several price points; when in doubt, undersell. Suggested steps include asking the guest how the issue can be made right.

Rejected wine: apologize and remove glass and bottle; away from the table, determine the condition; flawed: offer another bottle of the same wine; sound: offer the list; never put the guest in the position of being wrong. Wrong bottle or price on the check: bring in upper management. Pricing complaints: acknowledge and tactfully state the restaurant's pricing policy.
Food and beverage pairing: align with the guest's preferences first; if a guest prefers red wine with shellfish, the sommelier should honor that preference.
At the Advanced practical, candidates must deal with uncomfortable situations; some MSs may portray confrontational guests, reading from a script.

Code of Ethics (Integrity): knowingly and willfully serving counterfeit wines, or changing or replacing beverages served from preopened bottles, and materially misrepresenting the quality, condition or salability of a wine for gain are listed as problematic behavior.

unverified: The Court's MS page asks for 'proper serving portions' of spirits but publishes no figures. The NIAAA standard-drink sizes are shown as a reference only, not as Court or house portions.
The Curriculum Guide gives 2 oz as the usual sweet and fortified pour but prints two different metric conversions (59.1 ml and 51.9 ml); only the 2 oz figure is used.
The Court's 2-, 4- and 10-year Armagnac ages in the Curriculum Guide were not checked against Armagnac's own body; Armagnac ages are not stated here.
The 2025 standards say decanting can raise a wine's temperature by '1 to 3 degrees' without a unit; the figure is not used.
The Court's example MS feedback report is a template with placeholder names and scores; it is used only for the parts it lists, not as the exact structure of every exam.

read.stopsTitle: Four moves at the start of the meal

stops.name: Find the host
stops.text: Before anything, find the **host**, the guest leading the table. Stand to the right of whoever orders and repeat the order back.

stops.name: Know the product
stops.text: US **aperitif wine** is grape wine with added brandy or alcohol, flavored with herbs, at **15%** or more. **Vermouth** is one type. Be ready to say what's in it.

stops.name: Choose the service
stops.text: Pour at the **side station** with a jigger, **tableside** from the bottle, or from a **gueridon** in full view. Ask first: neat, over ice, with a water back?

stops.name: Cocktails
stops.text: Shake, stir or build to the recipe. Strain over **fresh ice**, never the shaker's "dirty rocks", and add bubbles after shaking, never before.

read.bigIdea: Right glass, right spot, every guest.
read.where: The Master practical asks you to **select, prepare and position glassware** for every drink, in the **lounge**, the **dining room** or a **private function room**. The rules hold everywhere: a tray, your right hand, the guest's right.

stops.name: Placement
stops.text: Same position for every guest, usually by the **knife**. Start with the **host** or the guest to the host's left, then go **clockwise**. Several glasses sit in a **line, diagonal, diamond or cluster**.

stops.name: Wine and sparkling
stops.text: Sparkling goes in **flutes or wine glasses**, as the guest prefers. A **second bottle** of the same wine gets a clean tasting glass for the host, to the right of the first.

stops.name: Spirits and fortified
stops.text: **Copita** or small tulip for fortified wine, grappa, eau de vie and neat liqueurs. **Rocks** for anything over ice. **Snifter** for neat oak-aged spirits.

stops.name: Beer and sake
stops.text: Match the beer glass to the style; an **AP wine glass** suits many. Modern sake service uses AP or white wine glasses; traditional service uses an **ochoko** in a **masu**.

stops.name: The setup
stops.text: Sparkling needs **two serviettes** and **two underliners** (bottle, cork). Decanting for sediment needs **three serviettes** and **three underliners** (cork, bottle, decanter).

read.mixup: A **snifter** is for neat, oak-aged spirits. A **copita** is for fortified wine, grappa and eau de vie. Over ice, use a **rocks** glass.
read.sayIt: I'll set a fresh glass so you can taste the new bottle first.

stops.text: US rules: distilled from **fruit** juice, mash or wine, bottled at **40%** or more. Grape brandy under **2 years** in oak is "immature brandy." **Cognac**, **Armagnac**, **Calvados** and **Pisco** follow their home country's law.

read.bigIdea: The guest leaves feeling right, every time.
read.where: At Master level, **questions and complaints** are handled with **skill, elegance and diplomacy**. At Advanced, the Court warns that examiners may play **confrontational guests** from a script.

stops.name: Three steps
stops.text: **Acknowledge** and listen. **Apologize** for how it felt. **Act** quickly and kindly. From Level 2: the longer version also asks the guest how to make it right.

stops.name: A rejected bottle
stops.text: Apologize, remove it and check it **away from the table**. Flawed: another bottle of the same. Sound: the list. Never put the guest in the position of being **wrong**.

stops.name: Price and the check
stops.text: A **wrong bottle or price** on the check goes to upper management. A complaint about list prices: acknowledge it and tactfully explain the house **pricing policy**.

stops.name: Selling with care
stops.text: Find the **budget** discreetly, offer several price points, and when in doubt **undersell**. A pricier suggestion needs a clear reason. Pairing starts with the guest: if they want red with shellfish, honor it.

stops.name: Honesty
stops.text: Never guess; offer to find out. The Court's **Code of Ethics** treats knowingly serving counterfeit wine, swapping a pre-opened bottle or misstating a wine's condition as breaches of **integrity**.

read.mixup: A **flawed** wine is replaced with another bottle of the **same** wine. A **sound** wine the guest doesn't like goes back for a new choice from the list.
read.sayIt: I'm sorry about that. Let me take it away and look after it.
